subject: History
chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
central_question: How do texts, inscriptions and archaeology reveal both social norms and the varied practices of kinship, caste, gender and class in early Indian societies?
in_scope_units: The Critical Edition of the Mahabharata and textual variation.
Families, kinship terminology and the ideal of patriliny.
Marriage rules, forms of marriage and women's gotra.
Satavahana metronymics and variations in kinship practice.
Varna occupations, non-Kshatriya rulers, jatis and social mobility.
Integration and exclusion beyond the four-varna framework.
Gendered access to property, varna and wealth.
Generosity and alternative forms of social status.
Historical analysis, composition and archaeology of the Mahabharata.
The epic as a dynamic text through regional and modern retellings.
banned_topics: Detailed formation of mahajanapadas and Mauryan administration, treated in the previous chapter.
Doctrines and monuments of Buddhism and Jainism, treated in the next chapter.

known_pitfalls.claim: Brahmanical prescriptions describe exactly how everyone lived.
known_pitfalls.correction: They express norms; inscriptions, other texts and stories show substantial regional and social variation.

known_pitfalls.claim: Satavahana metronymics prove that succession was matrilineal.
known_pitfalls.correction: Rulers used names derived from mothers, but succession was generally patrilineal.

known_pitfalls.claim: All early kings were Kshatriyas by birth.
known_pitfalls.correction: Several ruling lineages had other or contested origins, and power depended on support and resources rather than only prescribed varna.

recommended_example_progression: NCERT Exercise 7 on the Mahabharata's authorship.
NCERT Exercise 4 on the Buddhist social contract.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter ends with questions 1-5 in the 100-150 word section, essay questions 6-9, Map work 10 and Projects 11-12.
